Notably, a corner that is a saddle point on the full phase torus can appear as a local maximum or minimum along different time-evolution trajectories.

title: From The Unknown To The Desired: Transforming Unknown Initial States In The Resource Theory Of Work And Heat
authors: Andreas Winter Tanmoy Biswas
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09352v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study thermodynamic state transformations in the resource theory of work and heat when the initial quantum state is unknown. Moving beyond state-dependent protocols, we develop a universal framework in which a single transformation applies to all admissible input states. For mutually commuting conserved charges, we construct charge-conserving protocols whose transformation error, quantified by trace distance, decays super-polynomially with the number of system copies. As an application, we demonstrate universal work extraction: asymptotically optimal work can be extracted without microscopic knowledge of the initial state, with a super-polynomially small error. Our results show that thermodynamic state transformations remain achievable under limited prior information and establish a universal framework for resource-theoretic thermodynamics beyond the state-aware setting.
tldr: The paper develops a universal framework for thermodynamic state transformations in the resource theory of work and heat when the initial quantum state is unknown, achieving super-polynomially small error.
motivation: Standard thermodynamic protocols assume full knowledge of the initial state, which is unrealistic in many practical settings; this work addresses how to perform state transformations and work extraction under limited prior information.
method: For mutually commuting conserved charges, the authors construct charge-conserving protocols that apply a single transformation to all admissible input states, with transformation error measured by trace distance and decaying super-polynomially in the number of copies.
result: Asymptotically optimal work extraction is demonstrated without microscopic knowledge of the initial state, with super-polynomially small error, showing that thermodynamic transformations remain achievable under limited information.
conclusion: The results establish a universal framework for resource-theoretic thermodynamics beyond the state-aware setting, broadening the applicability of quantum thermodynamic protocols.

title: Bell Tests For Collider Decay Processes
authors: Danilo M. Fucci, Alexandre C. Orthey Jr., Alan J. Barr, Christopher G. Timpson
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09294v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose Bell tests for collider decays using independently sampled analysis axes as settings and detector regions to assign binary or null outcomes. We show that a Bell violation requires postselection, opening a loophole. However, under measurement independence and operational equivalence of acceptance events across settings, any local model exploiting the loophole must be nonclassical in the sense of measurement contextuality. We derive a Bell inequality violated by singlet correlations when the effective spin-analyzing powers are sufficiently high. Its violation then witnesses Bell nonlocality or measurement contextuality.
tldr: The paper proposes Bell tests for collider decay processes using independently sampled analysis axes as settings and detector regions as outcomes, showing that any Bell violation requires postselection—opening a loophole—but under measurement independence the loophole implies measurement contextuality.
motivation: To extend Bell tests beyond traditional quantum optics into high-energy collider decays, and to clarify whether observed correlations can witness Bell nonlocality or only measurement contextuality.
method: The authors use independently sampled analysis axes as measurement settings and detector regions to assign binary or null outcomes, derive a Bell inequality for singlet correlations when effective spin-analyzing powers are sufficiently high, and analyze the role of postselection and measurement independence.
result: They find that a Bell violation requires postselection, creating a loophole; however, under measurement independence and operational equivalence of acceptance events, any local model exploiting the loophole must be nonclassical in the sense of measurement contextuality. The derived Bell inequality is violated by singlet correlations when the effective spin-analyzing powers are high enough.
conclusion: Violation of the derived inequality witnesses either Bell nonlocality or measurement contextuality, offering a framework for Bell tests in collider decay processes and highlighting the need to address the postselection loophole.

title: From Certifying Rank $k$ Projectors To Non-Positivity, Entanglement, And Non-Hermitian Witnesses Through Traces Of Matrix Powers
authors: H. F. Chau
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We all know that a density matrix [MATH] is pure if and only if [MATH]. But is this the only way to prove the purity of [MATH] using the trace of its powers? Here I systematically study the necessary and sufficient conditions of the more general question of guaranteeing that all eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix belong to a specified set through its trace of powers. More importantly, these characterization results are automatically witnesses certifying a quantum state as entangled, a Hermitian operator has least one negative eigenvalue and a linear operator as non-Hermitian. I demonstrate the effectiveness of these witnesses, analyze their performance, and study their strength, weakness together with resource requirement through numerical simulation as well as analytical work. I also discuss briefly the effects of numerical stability, uncertainty in measurement and rounding errors on these problems.
tldr: The paper develops necessary and sufficient conditions on traces of matrix powers to certify that all eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix lie in a specified set, and applies these to construct witnesses for rank-k projectors, non-positivity, entanglement, and non-Hermiticity.
motivation: Purity testing via Tr(ρ^2) is a limited tool; there is a need for systematic trace-power conditions that can certify spectral properties and serve as practical witnesses for entanglement and non-Hermitian operators.
method: The author derives necessary and sufficient conditions on traces of powers for eigenvalue constraints of Hermitian matrices, then constructs witnesses and analyzes their performance, strength, weaknesses, resource requirements, numerical stability, and measurement uncertainty through numerical simulations and analytical work.
result: The characterization yields witnesses that effectively certify rank-k projectors, negative eigenvalues, entanglement, and non-Hermitianity, with numerical and analytical demonstrations of their performance and resource demands.
conclusion: Trace-power-based witnesses provide a versatile framework for spectral certification and entanglement detection, though practical implementation must account for numerical stability and measurement/rounding errors.

These characterization results are then reinterpreted as witnesses for entanglement, for the presence of at least one negative eigenvalue, and for non-Hermiticity of a linear operator. The work includes analytical derivations, numerical simulations to assess witness performance, and a discussion of practical issues such as numerical stability, measurement uncertainty, and rounding errors. title: Thermal Quantum Sensing: Fisher Information And Work Beyond Gaussian Signals
authors: Yash Chitgopekar, Nikolaos Koukoulekidis, Iman Marvian
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding how thermal fluctuations modify or suppress quantum-enhanced sensing is a central problem in quantum metrology. Closely related questions arise in quantum thermodynamics, particularly regarding the relation between the work induced by a signal and the information acquired by a sensor. Here, we establish general relations among the sensitivity of thermal quantum states, as quantified by different quantum Fisher information metrics, their temperature dependence, and the work induced by a unitary signal. We further show that, at high temperature, all monotone QFI metrics coincide to leading order with a universal quantity that can be expressed as the variance of a simple observable and itself defines a lesser-known QFI metric. This emergent uniqueness is reminiscent of the uniqueness of classical Fisher information in information geometry. In continuous-variable systems, the infinite-temperature limit is finite and generically non-zero for quadratic Gaussian signals, while it diverges for higher-degree signals. Remarkably, for any purely quadratic signal generator, the infinite-temperature QFI is at least twice the zero-temperature SLD QFI or, equivalently, at least eight times the ground-state variance of the generator. Consequently, the Cram\'er--Rao lower bound on the estimator variance is reduced by at least a factor of two. We illustrate these results using harmonic chains of bosonic modes relevant to trapped-ion platforms and quantum field-theoretic models.
tldr: The paper establishes universal relations between the quantum Fisher information of thermal states, their temperature dependence, and the work induced by a unitary signal, showing that at high temperature all monotone QFI metrics collapse onto a single emergent metric.
motivation: Thermal fluctuations can suppress quantum-enhanced sensing, and there is a deep but underexplored link between the thermodynamic work imparted by a signal and the information a quantum sensor acquires. Understanding this connection is central to both quantum metrology and quantum thermodynamics.
method: The authors derive general relations among monotone quantum Fisher information metrics, temperature, and signal-induced work for thermal states, and analyze continuous-variable systems (harmonic bosonic chains, quantum field models) to characterize Gaussian versus higher-degree signal generators.
result: At high temperature all monotone QFI metrics coincide to leading order with a universal quantity expressible as the variance of a simple observable; for quadratic Gaussian signals the infinite-temperature QFI is finite and at least twice the zero-temperature SLD QFI, reducing the Cramér-Rao bound by at least a factor of two.
conclusion: The emergent high-temperature uniqueness of the QFI metric mirrors the uniqueness of classical Fisher information in information geometry, revealing that thermal noise can counterintuitively enhance sensitivity for quadratic signals and linking sensing performance directly to thermodynamic work.

deep_read.detailed_summary:
This paper investigates how thermal fluctuations affect the performance of quantum sensors, focusing on the quantum Fisher information (QFI) of thermal states and its relation to the work induced by a unitary signal. The authors derive general relations among different QFI metrics—specifically the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) QFI, the right logarithmic derivative (RLD) QFI, and the anti-symmetric logarithmic derivative (ALD) QFI—and show that at high temperatures, all monotone QFI metrics coincide to leading order with a universal quantity. This universal quantity is expressed as the variance of a simple observable and itself defines a lesser-known QFI metric. The work bridges quantum metrology and quantum thermodynamics by connecting sensitivity to the work induced by a signal, providing a thermodynamic perspective on sensing.

The paper extends these results to continuous-variable systems, demonstrating that the infinite-temperature limit of the QFI is finite and generically non-zero for quadratic Gaussian signals, while it diverges for higher-degree signals. A key result is that for any purely quadratic signal generator, the infinite-temperature QFI is at least twice the zero-temperature SLD QFI, or equivalently at least eight times the ground-state variance of the generator. This implies that the Cramér–Rao lower bound on estimator variance is reduced by at least a factor of two at high temperature compared to zero temperature. The authors illustrate their findings using harmonic chains of bosonic modes, relevant to trapped-ion platforms and quantum field-theoretic models.

The analysis is comprehensive, spanning 77 pages with 10 figures, and provides a unified framework for understanding thermal effects in quantum sensing. The emergent uniqueness of the high-temperature QFI metric is reminiscent of the uniqueness of classical Fisher information in information geometry, suggesting a deep connection between quantum and classical estimation theory. The results have implications for practical quantum sensing in noisy, thermal environments and for the design of optimal sensors.

They define and compare various QFI metrics—SLD, RLD, and ALD—for thermal states, which are described by Gibbs density matrices. By expanding these metrics in the high-temperature limit, they identify a universal leading-order term that is common to all monotone QFI metrics. This term is expressed as the variance of an observable related to the signal generator. The analysis is extended to continuous-variable systems, where the signal generator is a polynomial in canonical operators. The authors use Gaussian state formalism to compute the QFI for quadratic generators and analyze the divergence for higher-degree generators. deep_read.results_analysis: The key results include the unification of QFI metrics at high temperature, where all monotone QFI metrics converge to a universal quantity given by the variance of a simple observable. For continuous-variable systems, the infinite-temperature QFI is finite and non-zero for quadratic Gaussian signals, with a specific lower bound: the infinite-temperature QFI is at least twice the zero-temperature SLD QFI, or at least eight times the ground-state variance of the generator. This implies a reduction of the Cramér–Rao lower bound by at least a factor of two. For higher-degree signals, the QFI diverges at infinite temperature, indicating that such signals become infinitely sensitive in the high-temperature limit, though this may be an artifact of the model. title: Energy Transport Structure And Fluctuation Theorem In Nonreciprocal Harmonic Chains
authors: Ziwei Cheng, Geng Li, Zhanchun Tu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonreciprocal interactions fundamentally alter energy transport by breaking the symmetry between forward and backward responses. Here, we uncover an exact transport structure for a one-dimensional harmonic chain with asymmetric nearest-neighbor couplings. Using a Green-function approach, we demonstrate that the direction of heat transport is determined not solely by the temperature bias, but by its competition with an effective directional asymmetry. This competition can reverse the direction of heat flow, enabling cold-to-hot transport. We further show that nonreciprocity introduces an additional power channel associated with the antisymmetric sector of the interaction, leading to a generalized steady-state energy balance involving two reservoir heat currents and a nonreciprocal power current. At the fluctuation level, the heat exchanges with the two reservoirs constitute correlated yet distinct stochastic currents, whose joint scaled cumulant generating function obeys an exact Gallavotti-Cohen symmetry. Together, these results establish a unified energetic and fluctuation framework for nonreciprocal heat transport and demonstrate that directional interactions can serve as an active resource for controlling nonequilibrium energy flows.

result: Heat flow direction is determined by competition between temperature bias and an effective directional asymmetry, which can reverse the current; nonreciprocity introduces an additional power channel from the antisymmetric interaction sector, and the joint fluctuations obey an exact Gallavotti-Cohen symmetry.
conclusion: Nonreciprocal interactions provide an active resource for controlling nonequilibrium energy flows, and the work establishes a unified energetic and fluctuation framework for nonreciprocal heat transport.

title: Information-geometric Bounds On Nonequilibrium Relaxation In Quantum Markov Dynamics
authors: Zhiqiang Huang Xiao-Kan Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study the quantum information-geometric structure underlying short-time nonequilibrium relaxation in quantum Markov dynamics, and derive bounds on the nonequilibrium correction to the short-time relaxation curvature. These bounds generalize the information-geometric structure underlying Auconi's classical nonequilibrium relaxation inequality to quantum Markov dynamics. We consider the von Neumann relative entropy as quantum divergence, and parametrize perturbations through the Kubo-Mori map, which converts the second-order expansion of the relative entropy into the Bogoliubov-Kubo-Mori (BKM) inner product at all temperatures. For a quantum Markov semigroup with full-rank stationary state, the induced tangent-space generator admits a canonical decomposition into a BKM-symmetric and a BKM-antisymmetric part, and the leading nonequilibrium curvature correction takes the exact form of the expectation of the commutator between the dissipative and the transport part of the generator. This correction is bounded by the product of a BKM-symmetric dissipative activity and a transport-sector activity. The bound is verified on a noncommuting qubit model and a driven-dissipative qutrit, and the full chain is confirmed numerically on a two-dimensional Fokker-Planck steady state. In the high-temperature and overdamped limit the quantum formula reduces to the position-space Fokker-Planck expression and reproduces Auconi's entropy-production bound with the correct temperature factor.

motivation: Understanding nonequilibrium relaxation and entropy production in quantum Markov dynamics and extending classical information-geometric inequalities to the quantum regime.
method: Uses von Neumann relative entropy and the Kubo-Mori map to define a Bogoliubov-Kubo-Mori inner product, then decomposes the tangent-space generator of a quantum Markov semigroup into symmetric and antisymmetric parts.

conclusion: Provides a quantum generalization of Auconi's classical nonequilibrium relaxation inequality, linking information geometry to thermodynamic bounds in quantum Markov dynamics.

title: Certifying Bipartite Entanglement On A Superconducting Processor From A Corrected Qaoa Cost Layer
authors: Carlos-Miguel Lorenzo
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm is the canonical near-term heuristic, yet on real superconducting hardware its behaviour is set by device physics, not by the algorithm. Hardware demonstrations rarely prove the intended coupling is realised, that genuine entanglement is prepared, or what controls it. We report a pre-registered single-device study on the nine-qubit superconducting processor Red at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center, using its five-qubit component. Across six calibrations we certify bipartite entanglement of a corrected QAOA cost layer on the good coupler at depth one by two-qubit tomographic negativity: 0.077, BCa 95% CI [0.065, 0.091], excluding zero every day, while the coupling-off twin stays separable and the degraded coupler equals zero. We then measure the device physics directly: in a pre-registered manipulation on a fixed Bell preparation (not the QAOA layer), reducing the CZ pulse amplitude causally reduces the certified negativity along a positive, well-fit slope (R^2 = 0.83-0.96), every rung-level interval excluding zero and surviving Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. This is a local linearisation of a peaked response, not a global monotone law: the negativity peaks at conditional phase |zeta| = pi, which the nominal amplitude overshoots. The J=0 twin is a separate off-state control and the fringe visibility is constant, so the effect is coherent. The average gate fidelity is non-monotone in the drive and is reported only as a diagnostic. A per-circuit statevector guardrail excludes a diagonal compilation fault we disclose and repair. A randomized-measurement witness is consistent with entanglement but underpowered. The certificate collapses by depth three, and a pre-registered sixteen-instance depth-three ensemble shows no optimisation signal (one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.15). We claim no advantage; the instances are classically trivial.
tldr: A pre-registered study on a superconducting processor certifies bipartite entanglement of a corrected QAOA cost layer via tomographic negativity and links it to CZ pulse amplitude.
motivation: QAOA on superconducting hardware often lacks proof that the intended coupling and genuine entanglement are realized; this work aims to certify entanglement and identify the device physics that controls it.
method: Using a five-qubit component, they perform two-qubit tomography to measure negativity across six calibrations, and manipulate CZ pulse amplitude on a fixed Bell state to correlate entanglement with gate calibration.
result: They find that negativity is maximized at a specific CZ pulse amplitude and that the corrected QAOA cost layer produces entangled states, demonstrating a route to verify entanglement in variational algorithms.

title: Non-Multiplicativity Of The Holevo Barycenter Of Quantum Channels
authors: Sayantan Chakraborty, Stefano Mancini, Leonardo Rossetti, Andreas Winter
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Holevo barycenter of a quantum channel is the unique output state obtained as the average output of any ensemble achieving the Holevo capacity. Given two quantum channels, the multiplicativity problem asks whether this barycenter tensorizes under parallel composition, namely whether the barycenter of the product channel coincides with the tensor product of the individual barycenters. This question is closely related to the additivity problem for the Holevo capacity: additivity implies tensorization of the Holevo barycenter, while tensorization alone is not sufficient for additivity. Although a construction is known that demonstrates the existence of channels with non-additive Holevo capacity, their corresponding Holevo barycenters still tensorize, leaving open whether multiplicativity might ultimately hold universally. Here, we answer this question in the negative by exhibiting channels for which the Holevo barycenter is not multiplicative under the tensor product of the channel with itself. Moreover, we show that the entropy of the Holevo barycenter is neither universally subadditive nor universally superadditive under tensor product.

method: The authors construct explicit quantum channels and analyze the Holevo barycenter of the channel tensored with itself, studying its entropy under parallel composition.
result: They exhibit channels whose Holevo barycenter is not multiplicative, and show that the entropy of the Holevo barycenter is neither universally subadditive nor universally superadditive.
conclusion: Multiplicativity of the Holevo barycenter fails in general, resolving a question left open by previous non-additivity constructions and revealing no universal entropy additivity for this quantity.

abstract: ArXiv:2609.09690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonreciprocal quantum batteries harness reservoir engineering for controlled energy transfer, heralding a paradigm shift for quantum energy storage. A prior study utilizing the Metelmann-Clerk formalism reported a fourfold enhancement in nonreciprocal energy accumulation over reciprocal counterparts. This fourfold enhancement, however, appears to stem from a Lindblad master equation that exhibits fundamental inconsistencies, which may systematically understate the actual nonreciprocal advantage. Our approach is rooted in the rigorously established cascaded open quantum systems formalism, which ensures both mathematical consistency and physical fidelity. Remarkably, we surpass the previously reported fourfold benchmark, attaining a regime-independent sixteenfold steady-state nonreciprocal energy advantage over reciprocal systems. We further uncover a dissipation-dependent battery-to-charger efficiency, fourfold under symmetric damping, surpassing this benchmark when the battery is less dissipative, and lower otherwise. This work establishes the cascaded formalism as a mathematically rigorous and experimentally viable foundation for high-performance quantum energy storage.
tldr: The paper develops a cascaded open quantum systems formalism for nonreciprocal quantum batteries, achieving a sixteenfold steady-state energy advantage and analyzing dissipation-dependent efficiency.
motivation: Quantum batteries promise improved energy storage via reservoir engineering, but prior nonreciprocal proposals using the Metelmann-Clerk formalism may be inconsistent and understate the achievable advantage.
method: The authors employ the rigorously established cascaded open quantum systems formalism to model nonreciprocal energy transfer, ensuring mathematical consistency and physical fidelity.
result: They obtain a regime-independent sixteenfold steady-state nonreciprocal energy advantage over reciprocal systems, surpassing the previous fourfold benchmark, and find a dissipation-dependent battery-to-charger efficiency that can exceed this benchmark when the battery is less dissipative.
conclusion: The cascaded formalism provides a mathematically rigorous and experimentally viable foundation for high-performance nonreciprocal quantum energy storage.

title: Execution-transcript Privacy For Fault-tolerant Surface-code Memories
authors: Hui Zhong Jiachen Shen (university Of Houston)
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A fault-tolerant quantum computer runs behind a telemetry stream logging syndromes, decoder actions, resets and timing separately from the answer. Can it reveal the logical input? For a distance-[MATH] rotated surface-code memory on a fixed schedule of [MATH] rounds, under three stated hypotheses (sector-scalar honest backbone, transcript locality, Kotecky-Preiss smallness), the channel from logical qubit to transcript is [MATH]-close in diamond norm to one that ignores the input. A statement of this kind follows generically from correctability-privacy duality. Anisotropy does not. Each logical axis pays the distance of its own coset, so under amplitude damping the computational-basis label is governed by the code's [MATH]-distance [MATH] and not by the code distance. Two codes of quantum distance [MATH] make the gap concrete. A phase-flip code's [MATH]-syndrome transcript is exactly input-independent under unobserved damping, while a repetition code leaks at first order. A matched converse identifies the records that do expose it, among them a lattice-surgery parity readout. On a 156-qubit superconducting processor our sufficient certificate misses by [MATH], so the theorem cannot be invoked there. Measured directly, a [MATH] memory's record identifies its input with total variation [MATH] under randomised, label-balanced acquisition. Holding the code fixed and varying the damping exposure reproduces the parameter-free law, with exponent [MATH] against a predicted [MATH]. Randomized encoding returns the statistic to the floor at no two-qubit-gate cost. Fault tolerance does not grant transcript privacy. It relocates it, and only to the logical state, not to the circuit's identity.
tldr: The paper studies whether telemetry transcripts from fault-tolerant surface-code memories leak the encoded logical input, showing that privacy depends on directional code distance and damping exposure rather than fault tolerance alone.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computers generate execution transcripts containing syndromes, decoder actions, resets, and timing; it is important to know whether such records can reveal the logical input.
method: Under three hypotheses, the logical-qubit-to-transcript channel is bounded in diamond norm by an input-independent channel, and leakage is analyzed for surface-code and repetition/phase-flip codes under amplitude damping, with experiments on a 156-qubit processor.

conclusion: Fault tolerance does not guarantee transcript privacy; it instead relocates the privacy requirement to the logical state and away from the circuit's identity, with randomized encoding restoring privacy at no two-qubit-gate cost.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates whether the telemetry stream of a fault-tolerant quantum computer—syndromes, decoder actions, resets, and timing—can leak the logical input state. Focusing on a distance-d rotated surface-code memory running for T=Θ(d) rounds, the authors prove that under three hypotheses (sector-scalar honest backbone, transcript locality, and Kotecky-Preiss smallness), the channel from logical qubit to transcript is e^{-Θ(d)}-close in diamond norm to a channel that completely ignores the input. This establishes a generic privacy guarantee for fault-tolerant architectures. However, the paper shows that this privacy is anisotropic: each logical axis is protected only by the distance of its own coset. Under amplitude damping, the computational-basis label is governed by the code's Z-distance d_Z, which can be as small as 1 even when the code distance d_min is larger. The authors illustrate this with two quantum distance-1 codes: a phase-flip code whose X-syndrome transcript is exactly input-independent under unobserved damping, and a repetition code that leaks at first order. They also provide a matched converse identifying which records do expose the input, including lattice-surgery parity readouts. Experimentally, on a 156-qubit superconducting processor, they find that their sufficient certificate for privacy misses by a factor of 21.5, meaning the theorem cannot be invoked for that device. Direct measurements on a d_Z=1 memory show that the record identifies the input with total variation ≥ 0.927 under randomized, label-balanced acquisition. Varying the damping exposure reproduces a parameter-free law with exponent 0.85±0.03 versus a predicted 0.86. Randomized encoding restores the statistic to the floor at no two-qubit-gate cost. The paper concludes that fault tolerance does not grant transcript privacy; it relocates it, and only to the logical state, not to the circuit's identity.

title: Conditions For Global Optimality In Quantum Arimoto-Blahut Algorithms
authors: Masahito Hayashi Geng Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generalized Arimoto--Blahut (AB) algorithms are widely used in information theory and quantum optimization, but monotonic objective decrease and numerical stabilization do not guarantee global optimality. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the global optimality of full-rank AB fixed points for convex differentiable objectives under linear constraints. An AB fixed point is globally optimal if and only if the AB update direction and the objective gradient differ by an element of the constraint normal space at that point. The same compatibility condition characterizes agreement between individual AB and mirror-descent (MD) updates, whereas pathwise equivalence requires it along the entire common trajectory. Thus, an AB algorithm may follow a trajectory different from MD and still reach the global optimum. We also develop a posteriori optimality certificates based on feasible directional derivatives, including finite-difference upper bounds on the objective gap that require only objective evaluations. For channel relative entropy between dephasing and depolarizing channels, we analytically identify the global minimizer as the unique full-rank AB fixed point, although pathwise equivalence fails. Numerical experiments illustrate convergence of AB and MD along different trajectories and validate the certificates. By contrast, an amplitude-damping example shows that a monotone AB iteration can stabilize at a suboptimal fixed point, whose nonoptimality is detected by the finite-difference certificate. These results provide structural and computable criteria for assessing global optimality in quantum AB algorithms.
tldr: The paper establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for global optimality of full-rank Arimoto-Blahut fixed points in quantum optimization, with applications to channel relative entropy and computable optimality certificates.
motivation: Monotonic convergence and numerical stability of generalized Arimoto-Blahut algorithms do not guarantee global optimality, so structural criteria are needed to certify optimal solutions.
method: The authors derive compatibility conditions between AB update directions and objective gradients under linear constraints, relate them to mirror-descent updates, and develop a posteriori optimality certificates using feasible directional derivatives and finite-difference bounds.
result: They analytically identify the global minimizer for channel relative entropy between dephasing and depolarizing channels, show that pathwise equivalence with mirror descent can fail while global optimality still holds, and demonstrate a monotone AB iteration stabilizing at a suboptimal fixed point for an amplitude-damping example.
conclusion: These results provide computable and structural criteria for assessing global optimality in quantum Arimoto-Blahut algorithms, extending their theoretical foundations beyond monotonicity.

title: Certified Measurement And Control Of An Entanglement-breaking Index On Programmable Hardware
authors: Eran Kopel
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09350v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The entanglement-breaking index of a quantum channel, the number of self-compositions after which the channel destroys all entanglement with any reference, has to our knowledge never been measured. We show that a certified thermal collision feedback loop makes this integer both measurable and controllable on current programmable hardware, every load-bearing quantity delivered as an interval-arithmetic certificate. On the measurement side: a target list for the integer staircase n_EB(p) with decision-point negativities certified at margins 0.025 to 0.109; an exact per-round depolarising model in which the selected staircase survives realistic noise as certified integers; an exact, tight compilation of the round unitary (seven CNOTs all-to-all, five native arbitrary-angle gates, ten on heavy-hex); and a 33-million-draw gated search bounding the thermal valley's contrast by a wall with an interior maximum, a certified 2.85x10^-3 near floor 89. On the control side: the model composes rounds of differing bath polarisation exactly, so the valley becomes a pulsed valve, switching at a certified minimal pulse of exactly eight rounds; the optimal pulsed signal, a certified 3.43x10^-3, beats the static protocol, so the best valley measurement is intrinsically pulsed; and a coherent tilt of the bath Bloch vector lifts the signal to a certified 8.6x10^-3, three times the static ceiling, at zero population cost. Valley signatures certifiably die near per-round noise strength 10^-4, fixing the error-extrapolation burden. The staircase is a near-term experiment; the pulsed valley a precisely priced one.
tldr: The paper introduces a certified method to measure and control the entanglement-breaking index of a quantum channel on programmable quantum hardware using a thermal collision feedback loop.
motivation: The entanglement-breaking index, a previously unmeasured integer characterizing when a channel destroys all entanglement, is important for understanding quantum channel capacities and entanglement dynamics.
method: They use interval-arithmetic certificates and a thermal collision feedback loop to measure the staircase of entanglement-breaking indices, compiling exact round unitaries and analyzing noise and control via pulsed protocols.
result: They certify the integer staircase with decision-point negativities, bound the thermal valley's contrast, and demonstrate that pulsed control (including coherent bath tilt) beats static protocols, with signatures dying near per-round noise 10^-4.
conclusion: The staircase is a near-term experiment, and the pulsed valley is precisely priced, enabling certified measurement and control of entanglement-breaking on current hardware.

title: A Sum-of-Squares Hierarchy With Quadratic Convergence For Quantum Channel Coding
authors: Hoang Anh Tran Hoang Ta
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09629v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computing the optimal success probability for transmitting classical messages through a single use of a quantum channel is NP-hard, even for two messages. An existing semidefinite programming hierarchy based on symmetric extensions provides convergent upper bounds with an a priori error estimate that decays as the inverse square root of the extension level. In this work, we construct a Hermitian sum-of-squares hierarchy for an arbitrary number of messages and prove quadratic convergence in its level. The error bound is proportional to the advantage over random guessing. Our approach combines state-discrimination duality with positive polynomial kernels on products of spheres to construct feasible polynomial dual certificates. For binary messages, the resulting bounds give a multiplicative approximation from above of the trace-norm contraction coefficient.

title: Spectral Core-Tail Architecture For Locally Certified Gibbs-State Preparation
authors: Rui-Hao Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09291v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preparing a quantum Gibbs state requires reproducing both its thermal distribution and the associated many-body eigenspaces. In this work, we formalize the spectral core-tail architecture (SCTA) as a framework comprising a structured thermal core, a geometrically characterized unitary tail, and an exact residual measuring the remaining core-frame Hamiltonian mismatch. We derive a local Gibbs-state error bound separating core-preparation, tail-implementation, and modeling errors. The modeling contribution is volume uniform when its Kubo-Mori response meets the shell summability condition and the relevant local data remain uniform. We then highlight three anchor Hamiltonian classes which admit exact core-tail constructions with zero residuals. For small deformations of an exact anchor, we employ a Schrieffer-Wolff reduction procedure to construct a corrected core-tail pair that formally removes the deformation order by order. Under uniform locality and solvability assumptions, we show that the first-order reduction yields a residual that remains bounded and is quadratic in the deformation strength. Furthermore, we numerically test the first-order reduction on deformed graph-stabilizer Hamiltonians. The numerical results show approximately quadratic suppression of both the Hamiltonian-level mismatch and the local Gibbs-state error in the perturbative regime. We also find that the constructed correction circuit structure remains useful as a variational ansatz beyond perturbative control, often improving on both the bare and prescribed first-order states.

title: Exact Asymptotic Equivalence Between Precisions Of Record-times And Integrated Currents
authors: Alberto Garilli
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish an exact equivalence between the fluctuations of integrated currents and the temporal statistics of current record events in continuous-time Markov jump processes. The results are derived within a purely probabilistic framework and clarify the structural origin of current precision in terms of first-passage-like event statistics.

conclusion: Provides a unified representation of current fluctuations in terms of record-time observables and clarifies the structural origin of current precision through first-passage-like event statistics.

title: A Metastable State In $\mathrm{Yb}^+$ With Lifetime Greater Than 10 Minutes

abstract: ArXiv:2609.09523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We find through direct, time-domain measurement of trapped [MATH] ions that the excited [MATH] state has a collision-free lifetime of 17.8(6) min, long enough for use in atomic clockwork or quantum information processing. title: Distinguishability Transitions From Global Quantum Snapshots

title: Transient And Universal Regimes In Quantum Reaction-transport Kinetics

abstract: ArXiv:2609.09305v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum reaction-transport systems consist of coherently propagating particles that irreversibly react upon encounter. Consequently, fluctuations dominate the asymptotic kinetics for [MATH]. In one dimension, they render mean-field relaxation transient and drive the system toward a transport-limited regime with [MATH], governed by a quantum-Zeno scale even for arbitrarily weak loss. At [MATH], the kinetics acquires logarithmic corrections, whereas above two dimensions mean-field scaling is asymptotically restored. At and below the upper critical dimension, mean-field behavior can nevertheless persist over parametrically long crossover times before the asymptotic fluctuation-dominated regime emerges. The crossover times below D_c can be parametrically long, meaning mean-field behavior may be observed in experiments before the asymptotic regime sets in. Specific numerical values for crossover times or collision rates are not provided in the abstract, but the scaling exponents are clearly identified.

title: Josephson Energy Of Superconducting Junctions: Amorphous Versus Crystalline Tunnel Barriers

Scattering-state analysis shows that transport is quantum tunneling and that the variability originates from stoichiometric inhomogeneity of the amorphous oxide: Al-rich, low-barrier regions can connect into percolation-like tunneling pathways that strongly enhance the conductance. title: Realization Theory For Quantum Filtering: Classifying Continuously Monitored Bosonic Systems
authors: Jacob Emerson
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exact finite-dimensional descriptions exist for a few important classes of continuously monitored quantum systems, but there is no general criterion separating systems that admit such filters from those that do not. We formulate this question as a realization problem and introduce the linearized observable Hankel operator [MATH], which maps changes in the past measurement record to changes in a future conditional observable. For polynomial bosonic systems under continuous quadrature monitoring, this gives a sharp boundary between finite and infinite realizability. Gaussian dynamics and the Conditional Momentum Moment class admit exact finite-dimensional filters, while nonlinear dynamics outside these classes generically produce infinitely many independent response directions and admit no robust finite-dimensional [MATH] observable- or state-level filter. The singular values of [MATH] then extend the same realization framework to approximation, giving the optimal rank-[MATH] local-response error beyond the finite classes. Numerical experiments with the Kerr and Duffing oscillators, together with a dynamics-adapted Poisson--Charlier construction for Kerr dynamics, show how this observable-level benchmark interacts with concrete reduced representations. Together, these results identify the boundary of exact quantum filtering and quantify finite-dimensional approximation beyond it.

method: Introduces a linearized observable Hankel operator mapping changes in the past measurement record to changes in a future conditional observable, analyzed for polynomial bosonic systems under continuous quadrature monitoring, with numerical experiments on Kerr and Duffing oscillators.
result: A sharp boundary between finite and infinite realizability is established: Gaussian dynamics and the Conditional Momentum Moment class admit exact finite-dimensional filters, while nonlinear dynamics outside these classes generically yield infinitely many independent response directions and no robust finite-dimensional filter; singular values give the optimal rank-r local-response error.
conclusion: The work identifies the boundary of exact quantum filtering and quantifies finite-dimensional approximation beyond it, providing a benchmark for reduced representations of monitored bosonic systems.

title: Materials For Quantum Information Science: Roles In The Quantum Evolution 2.0
authors: Thang Pham, Vsevolod Ivanov, Dominic P. Goronzy, Abhiram Devata, Joshua Feldon, David Barton, You Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09371v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum information science is entering a second phase, the Quantum Evolution 2.0, in which the challenge has shifted from demonstrating coherent control of individual quantum states to building scalable multi-qubit processors and networks. This transition places materials science at the center of the field. Across superconducting circuits, quantum defects, quantum photonic devices, and emerging materials platforms, including two-dimensional materials and heterostructures, performance is now limited less by device design than by poorly controlled surfaces, buried interfaces, and defects whose atomic identities remain incompletely known. This review surveys the materials challenges of these quantum platforms together with the characterization methods needed to resolve them. For each platform we identify the dominant decoherence mechanisms, the current state of materials understanding, and the most pressing open materials problems. A cross-platform comparison then reveals a shared structure-coherence problem. The implicated material chemistry recurs across platforms, involving light elements in disordered or buried environments, yet no platform can quantitatively connect a specific atomic-scale structure to a measured change in coherence. We close by identifying three needs, mechanistic understanding of decoherence at the atomistic level, high-throughput proxy metrics predictive of device performance, and characterization tools built for quantum materials, whose resolution would advance coherence, scalability, and integration across all platforms.
tldr: This review surveys materials challenges across quantum information platforms, identifying surface/interface defects as a shared bottleneck for coherence and scalability.
motivation: As quantum information science shifts from single-qubit control to scalable processors and networks, materials imperfections such as uncontrolled surfaces, buried interfaces, and unknown defects increasingly limit device performance.
method: The authors review superconducting circuits, quantum defects, quantum photonic devices, and emerging 2D materials/heterostructures, comparing dominant decoherence mechanisms, materials understanding, and open problems across platforms.
result: They find a recurring structure-coherence problem involving light elements in disordered or buried environments, but no platform can yet quantitatively link a specific atomic-scale structure to a measured coherence change.
conclusion: The review identifies three key needs—atomistic understanding of decoherence, high-throughput proxy metrics, and quantum-specific characterization tools—to improve coherence, scalability, and integration across platforms.

title: Finite-energy Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill State-enhanced Optical Interferometry
authors: Ashmita Roy, R. Srikanth, Deepak Pandey
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the case of a Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) state-enhanced optical interferometry with detailed analysis of the phase sensitivity for both the SU(2) and SU(1,1) interferometers. The conventional quantum-enhanced SU(2) interferometer, employing coherent light at one input port and squeezed light at the other, is compared with a modified configuration using coherent light and a GKP state. While it is known that the squeezed vacuum state is the optimal Gaussian resource input mode when paired with the coherent state, we show that the finite-energy GKP state with sufficiently broad envelope outperforms the squeezed vacuum injection, irrespective of the presence of optical losses. This can be attributed to the enhanced robustness coming from the availability of multiple squeezed peaks in the GKP case. However, because lowering the mean photon number reduces the GKP envelope width, the squeezed vacuum input performs better when compared with a GKP state of equal or lower mean photon number. We also observe that optical losses tend to diminish the relative advantage of either input state, since both states approach the (unsqueezed) vacuum state asymptotically. Our work demonstrates the direct application of finite-energy GKP states in optical interferometry along with a methodology for estimating the quantum Fisher information (QFI) and presents a phase estimation procedure using non-Gaussian resources in comparison with conventional Gaussian states.
tldr: Analyzes finite-energy GKP-state-enhanced optical interferometry and shows that broad-envelope GKP inputs can outperform squeezed vacuum in phase sensitivity under loss, but not at equal or lower mean photon number.
motivation: To explore non-Gaussian GKP resources for quantum-enhanced metrology and assess their practical advantage over Gaussian states under realistic loss and energy constraints.

They find that for sufficiently broad GKP envelope (i.e., large mean photon number), the GKP state outperforms the squeezed vacuum even in the presence of optical losses, due to the multiple squeezed peaks inherent in the GKP state providing enhanced robustness. However, when the mean photon number is constrained to be equal or lower, the squeezed vacuum performs better because the GKP envelope width shrinks with decreasing photon number. Optical losses reduce the relative advantage of both non-classical states as they asymptotically approach the vacuum state. The work demonstrates a direct application of finite-energy GKP states in interferometry and provides a methodology for estimating QFI with non-Gaussian resources.

title: Induced Random Mixed States Are Symmetric Dirichlet Mixtures
authors: Brian T. Kirby, Alexander C. B. Greenwood, Sanjaya Lohani, Joseph M. Lukens
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09421v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish an exact equivalence in distribution between [MATH]-dimensional random mixed states induced by partial traces over [MATH]-dimensional environments and the Mai-Alquier distribution, a mixture of [MATH] independent Haar-random pure states weighted by a symmetric Dirichlet distribution. This identification recasts a class of expectation values for induced ensembles into calculations involving Dirichlet moments and low-order Haar averages on a single-system state space. As applications, we recover exact purity moments up to fourth order, derive the mean Hilbert--Schmidt distance between independent induced ensembles with possibly different environment dimensions, and obtain exact average determinants. These results provide a unified and constructive perspective on induced random mixed states and on the evaluation of quantities such as purity moments, overlaps, and determinants.
tldr: The paper proves that random mixed states induced by partial traces over an environment are exactly distributed as a symmetric Dirichlet mixture of Haar-random pure states, enabling exact calculations of purity moments, Hilbert-Schmidt distances, and determinants.
motivation: Random induced mixed states are widely used in quantum information, but their exact distributional properties are not fully characterized, which limits analytical calculations of ensemble averages.
method: The authors derive an exact distributional equivalence to the Mai-Alquier distribution and then use Dirichlet moments and low-order Haar averages on single-system state spaces to compute expectation values.
result: They recover exact purity moments up to fourth order, the mean Hilbert-Schmidt distance between independent induced ensembles with possibly different environment dimensions, and exact average determinants.
conclusion: This unified and constructive perspective facilitates evaluating quantities such as purity moments, overlaps, and determinants for induced random mixed states, with potential applications in quantum information theory.

deep_read.detailed_summary:

This identification is the central result and is proven constructively. The equivalence allows expectation values over the induced ensemble to be computed using Dirichlet moments and low-order Haar averages on a single D-dimensional system, avoiding direct integration over the full bipartite unitary group.

As applications, the authors recover exact purity moments up to fourth order, derive the mean Hilbert–Schmidt distance between independent induced ensembles with possibly different environment dimensions K and K', and obtain exact average determinants. The purity moments are expressed in closed form in terms of D and K, and the Hilbert–Schmidt distance formula generalizes previous results to unequal environment dimensions. The core methodology is a constructive probabilistic mapping. The authors show that a random mixed state ρ = Tr_K(|ψ⟩⟨ψ|), where |ψ⟩ is Haar-random on C^D ⊗ C^K, can be represented as ρ = ∑_{i=1}^K p_i |φ_i⟩⟨φ_i|, where the weights (p_1,...,p_K) follow a symmetric Dirichlet distribution with parameters (1,...,1) and the states |φ_i⟩ are independent Haar-random pure states on C^D. This representation is exact and follows from the properties of Haar measure and the Schmidt decomposition. The proof likely uses the fact that the eigenvalues of the reduced state are distributed as the squared singular values of a D×K random Gaussian matrix (or equivalently, as the eigenvalues of a Wishart matrix), which are known to follow a Dirichlet distribution after normalization. The independence of the eigenvector directions from the eigenvalues is also a standard result.

Once this equivalence is established, the computation of expectation values reduces to evaluating moments of the Dirichlet distribution and Haar averages over single-system pure states. For example, the purity P = Tr(ρ^2) can be written as ∑_{i,j} p_i p_j |⟨φ_i|φ_j⟩|^2, and its moments can be computed using known Dirichlet moments and the fact that ⟨|⟨φ_i|φ_j⟩|^2⟩ = 1/D for i≠j and 1 for i=j. title: Gap-controlled Thermalization In A Ssh Model Version Of The Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou Chain
authors: Gerardo G. Naumis Jos\'e A. Ak\'e
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09498v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In classical anharmonic lattices, the resonance structure driving nonlinear mode mixing is reshaped by band gaps. However, it remains unclear whether a spectral gap hinders or promotes long-time thermalization. Here we study a dimerized Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou chain - a classical SSH model analogue with alternating spring constants - and quantify how the acoustic-optical gap controls relaxation under alpha-type (cubic) nonlinearity. Tracking modal energies and spectral entropy via long-time symplectic simulations, we find a sharp isolation threshold when the dimerization strength reaches half its maximum value, set by the onset of the first umklapp process that allows two zone-boundary acoustic phonons to fuse into a zone-center optical phonon; below this threshold, three-wave acoustic-acoustic-optical scattering activates the optical branch on timescales of order 1e4 oscillation periods, while above it the bands remain dynamically isolated. We further show that boundary conditions reshape this picture, producing long-lived sticky states for specific mode excitations. These results establish the phononic gap as a tunable, momentum-selective filter for nonlinear energy transport, suggesting a general route to controlling thermalization in dimerized or topologically gapped nonlinear lattices.
tldr: The paper studies how the acoustic-optical gap in a dimerized classical Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou chain controls long-time thermalization and nonlinear energy transport.
motivation: It addresses the open question of whether a spectral gap hinders or promotes thermalization in anharmonic lattices, using a classical SSH-like model with alternating spring constants.
method: Long-time symplectic simulations track modal energies and spectral entropy in a dimerized FPU chain with cubic nonlinearity, identifying three-wave scattering processes and umklapp thresholds.
result: A sharp isolation threshold occurs when dimerization reaches half its maximum, below which acoustic-acoustic-optical scattering activates the optical branch on timescales of order 1e4 oscillation periods; boundary conditions can produce long-lived sticky states.
conclusion: The phononic gap acts as a tunable, momentum-selective filter for nonlinear energy transport, suggesting a general route to control thermalization in dimerized or topologically gapped nonlinear lattices.

title: Perfect State Transfer From A Localised Two-Excitation State To A Dicke State Via Static Spin-Network Hamiltonians
authors: Soumyojyoti Dutta
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09654v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I construct a family of time-independent, excitation-preserving spin Hamiltonians that realises perfect state transfer from a localised two-excitation state to the symmetric two-excitation Dicke state, for every system size [MATH]. The Hamiltonian has the physical form [MATH] exists; a subresultant argument supplies a real lift of that root to the original system. The existence proof is entirely symbolic and does not rely on numerical optimisation; direct propagation is used only as independent validation. The result is a constrained analogue of perfect state transfer: unlike the general real-state problem, where an unconstrained real symmetric matrix suffices, here the Hamiltonian is required to arise from an excitation-preserving spin-network form.
tldr: Constructs a family of time-independent excitation-preserving spin Hamiltonians that perfectly transfer a localized two-excitation state to a symmetric two-excitation Dicke state for arbitrary system size.
motivation: Perfect state transfer in spin networks is a fundamental primitive for quantum information transmission, but existing constructions often assume unconstrained Hamiltonians; this work enforces a physical excitation-preserving spin-network form.
method: A symbolic existence proof is given, using a subresultant argument to lift a real root to the original system, with direct propagation used only for independent numerical validation.
result: For every system size, a real Hamiltonian of the required spin-network form exists that achieves perfect state transfer from a localized two-excitation state to the Dicke state.
conclusion: The paper extends perfect state transfer to a physically constrained setting, broadening the class of realizable spin-network Hamiltonians that can achieve perfect transfer to Dicke states.

title: Fermionic Quantum Cellular Automata In 2d Are Trivial
authors: Jeffrey Kwan, David M. Long, Jeongwan Haah
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09317v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fermionic quantum cellular automata (QCA) are automorphisms of local fermionic operator algebras ([MATH]-graded superalgebras) that have bounded spread: they map local operators to nearby operators. We prove that every 2-dimensional fermionic QCA on a locally finite-dimensional algebra is a composition of local automorphisms and a fermionic shift. This is implied by our result that every locally finite-dimensional fermionic invertible subalgebra in a one-dimensional lattice is Brauer trivial, , it is stably bounded-spread isomorphic to a tensor product fermionic algebra.
tldr: The paper proves that every 2-dimensional fermionic quantum cellular automaton on locally finite-dimensional algebras is trivial, decomposing into local automorphisms and a fermionic shift.
motivation: Fermionic quantum cellular automata are bounded-spread automorphisms of local fermionic operator algebras, and their classification is important for understanding possible nontrivial fermionic quantum dynamics.
method: The authors use the algebraic framework of Z2-graded local fermionic operator algebras and prove that every locally finite-dimensional fermionic invertible subalgebra in a one-dimensional lattice is Brauer trivial.
result: Every 2D fermionic QCA on a locally finite-dimensional algebra is a composition of local automorphisms and a fermionic shift, and such one-dimensional fermionic invertible subalgebras are stably bounded-spread isomorphic to tensor-product fermionic algebras.
conclusion: Fermionic QCA in two dimensions are trivial in this classification sense, constraining their possible topological or nonlocal behavior beyond local automorphisms and shifts.

title: A Block Tensor Train Burer-Monteiro Framework For Low-Rank Quantum State Tomography
authors: Shakir Showkat Sofi, Charlotte Vermeylen, Fatemeh Mohammadi, Lieven de Lathauwer
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum state tomography is a fundamental technique for estimating the state of a quantum system from measured data and plays a crucial role in evaluating the performance of quantum devices. However, standard estimation methods become computationally prohibitive as the system size increases due to the exponential growth of the density matrix, describing a quantum state, with the number of qubits. We propose a low-rank tensor-network framework for mixed-state quantum state tomography based on a block tensor train (Block-TT) factorization. Specifically, the density matrix is represented as the contraction of a Block-TT with its Hermitian transpose, yielding a TT analogue of the Burer-Monteiro factorization. This parameterization guarantees Hermiticity and positive semidefiniteness by construction while compressing the number of optimization variables from exponential to linear in the number of qubits. Building on this representation, we develop single-site and two-site density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) algorithms for estimating quantum states from compressed measurements. The resulting methods operate directly on the compressed parameterization, support adaptive rank refinement, and exploit efficient tensor-network contractions for expectation-value evaluation. The framework is applicable to a broad class of low-rank quantum states, including pure states, nearly pure states, and ground states that admit accurate tensor-network approximations. Numerical experiments demonstrate accurate state reconstruction from limited measurements together with substantial reductions in memory requirements and computational cost compared with conventional low-rank tomography methods.
tldr: A low-rank block tensor train Burer-Monteiro framework for mixed-state quantum state tomography with DMRG algorithms that reduces optimization variables from exponential to linear in the number of qubits.
motivation: Standard quantum state tomography becomes computationally prohibitive as system size grows due to the exponential growth of the density matrix, motivating efficient low-rank tensor-network methods.
method: The density matrix is parameterized as the contraction of a Block-TT with its Hermitian transpose, guaranteeing Hermiticity and positive semidefiniteness, and single-site/two-site DMRG algorithms are developed for estimation from compressed measurements with adaptive rank refinement.
result: Numerical experiments demonstrate accurate state reconstruction from limited measurements together with substantial reductions in memory requirements and computational cost compared with conventional low-rank tomography methods.
conclusion: The framework applies to a broad class of low-rank quantum states, including pure, nearly pure, and ground states admitting accurate tensor-network approximations, enabling scalable quantum state tomography.

title: The Kernel-block Rank Profile And A Complete Classification Of $\mathbb{Z}_2\mathbb{Z}_4\mathbb{Z}_8$-linear Hadamard Codes

title: Dual-unitary Circuits As A Platform For Quantum Reservoir Computing
authors: Pieter W. Claeys Gabriel O. Alves
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) is a machine learning approach which employs the internal dynamics of a physical system (the reservoir) to encode and process information. In this work, we explore the use of dual-unitary circuits in a brickwork architecture as a platform for QRC, well suited to current noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. Dual-unitary circuits present both practical and conceptual advantages. Our results indicate that, under appropriate conditions, dual-unitarity can lead to an enhanced regime of operation: we numerically verify that it improves memory effects and nonlinear processing, and shields against finite-shot noise, mitigating exponential concentration. Moreover, dual unitarity offers an intuitive picture of how operator dynamics gives rise to memory and nonlinear processing in circuit-based reservoirs.
tldr: The paper proposes dual-unitary brickwork circuits as a platform for quantum reservoir computing, showing enhanced memory, nonlinear processing, and noise resilience under suitable conditions.
motivation: Quantum reservoir computing needs physical reservoirs with strong memory and nonlinear processing that remain robust on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.
method: The authors numerically study quantum reservoir computing with dual-unitary brickwork circuits, analyzing memory effects, nonlinear processing, finite-shot noise, and operator dynamics.
result: Dual-unitarity can improve memory and nonlinear processing and can shield against finite-shot noise by mitigating exponential concentration.
conclusion: Dual-unitary circuits offer practical and conceptual advantages for QRC and provide an intuitive operator-dynamics picture, though the work is primarily a quantum machine learning application rather than a core information-theoretic advance.

title: Python In The Front, Party In The Backline: Compiling Quantum Workloads Across CPUs, GPUs, And FPGAs
authors: Joseph K. L. Lee, Mehrdad Malekmohammadi, Hong-Sheng Zheng, Shuli Shu, Cheick Doumbia, Kalman Szenes, Mehran Zamani Abnili, Thomas Ainsworth, Matthew Seymour, Thomas Germain, Leonhard Neuhaus, Josh Izaac, Lee J. O'riordan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Moving from quantum research and development to production-grade, fault-tolerant quantum workload execution remains one of the most significant challenges facing quantum platform builders. While Python frameworks have enabled an easy entry point for quantum algorithm design, the low-latency requirements for real-time quantum error correction (QEC) demand performance that traditional interpreted environments cannot provide. FPGAs and ASICs play a central role at these layers, but their specialized programming models make development rigid and time-consuming. CPUs, GPUs, and other accelerators introduce a different challenge: as infrastructure becomes increasingly heterogeneous, programming across different devices and their associated abstractions becomes more complex. Allowing researchers to write workloads in high-level languages that map to low-latency execution across diverse distributed target platforms will enable the development of key infrastructure for utility-scale quantum systems. For this, we introduce [MATH], a heterogeneous compilation and runtime framework built within PennyLane and Catalyst. Backline allows us to design and build quantum-classical workloads for high-performance and low-latency devices, with compilation directly from a Python interface through MLIR. We demonstrate the compilation and execution of several quantum workloads with low-latency data movement across a mix of CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs, for both local and distributed remote hardware targets, all from a vendor-agnostic Python frontend. With an AMD VPK120 FPGA board as the controller, issuing each round from its hardware-handshake engine, we measured median steady-state round-trip latencies over RoCE v2 of [MATH]s to an AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO CPU and [MATH]s to an AMD Instinct MI210 GPU across [MATH] rounds per path, demonstrating microsecond-scale synchronous co-processing.
tldr: Backline is a heterogeneous MLIR-based compilation and runtime framework in PennyLane/Catalyst that compiles Python quantum workloads down to low-latency execution across CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs for real-time quantum error correction control.
motivation: Real-time QEC and production-grade fault-tolerant workload execution require microsecond latencies that interpreted Python frameworks cannot deliver, while FPGA/ASIC programming models are rigid and heterogeneous accelerators add programming complexity.
method: The authors build a vendor-agnostic Python frontend that lowers quantum-classical programs through MLIR to multiple backend targets, using an AMD VPK120 FPGA as a hardware-handshake controller issuing QEC rounds over RoCE v2 to CPU and GPU nodes.
result: They measured median steady-state round-trip latencies at microsecond scale (reported as redacted values) to an AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO CPU and an AMD Instinct MI210 GPU across thousands of rounds per path.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that a single high-level Python interface can drive synchronous, low-latency co-processing across distributed heterogeneous hardware, offering infrastructure relevant to utility-scale quantum control stacks.

title: The Geometry Of Transport In Quantum Walks And Parrondo's Paradox
authors: Jose Alfredo de Leon, Mariana P\'erez-Muralles, Jan Neuser, Carlos Pineda
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09269v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study Parrondo's paradox -- the phenomenon where combining losing strategies yields a winning one -- in a minimal discrete-time quantum walk. We introduce the transport vector, encoded in the coin's steady state, whose inner product with the initial coin state gives the walker's asymptotic velocity. More generally, the paradox emerges exactly when the transport vector of the combined strategy falls outside the cone spanned by the individual ones -- a geometric criterion valid for any combination of strategies. It explains, for instance, why composing two coin operators within a single step can produce the paradox while simple alternation between them cannot, since alternation keeps the combined vector confined to the cone. The paradoxical set has nonzero measure, and we compute its probability explicitly in representative cases. This casts the paradox as one instance of designing reachable transport in quantum walks.
tldr: The paper introduces a geometric transport vector to explain Parrondo's paradox in discrete-time quantum walks, showing the paradox occurs exactly when the combined strategy's transport vector lies outside the cone spanned by individual strategies.
motivation: To understand why combining losing quantum walk strategies can yield winning transport, and to provide a general geometric criterion for Parrondo's paradox.
method: The authors model a minimal discrete-time quantum walk, encode the walker's asymptotic velocity in a transport vector derived from the coin's steady state, and analyze combinations of coin operators.
result: The paradox emerges exactly when the combined transport vector falls outside the cone of individual vectors; the paradoxical set has nonzero measure, and its probability is computed explicitly in representative cases.
conclusion: This geometric perspective unifies Parrondo's paradox as a design principle for reachable transport in quantum walks, explaining why certain compositions produce the paradox while simple alternation does not.

title: Balancing Expressivity And Overfitting In Quantum Gaussian Process Regression
authors: Saasha Joshi, Udson C. Mendes, Luke C. G. Govia
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Active learning is a paradigm of machine learning that can be utilized to model expensive black-box functions by training a surrogate model from actively queried training points. The performance of this framework depends heavily on the choice of the surrogate model. When the surrogate is Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), its performance is largely determined by the expressivity of the underlying kernel. In this work, we investigate the peculiarities of using a quantum kernel to change the computational dynamics of active learning with GPR, focusing on the sensitivity to regularization by hyperparameter tuning. While generic, unstructured kernels suffer from exponential concentration at large scale, we empirically demonstrate that even at small scale overfitting can collapse GPR performance. Kernel regularization can be used to counteract this effect, but due to the smoothness of the quantum fidelity kernel, regularization must be carefully chosen to balance expressivity and overfitting. Our qualitative results transfer to the practical application of restricted quantum kernels designed to avoid exponential concentration and also present the kinds of noise that may be valuable to kernel training in near-term quantum devices.
tldr: The paper empirically studies how kernel expressivity and overfitting trade off when quantum fidelity kernels are used in Gaussian process regression for active learning, showing that regularization must be carefully tuned.
motivation: Active learning with GPR depends strongly on the surrogate kernel's expressivity, but it is unclear how quantum kernels behave in this setting and how sensitive performance is to hyperparameter-driven regularization.
method: The authors compare quantum kernels against generic unstructured kernels in GPR-based active learning, empirically analyzing overfitting at small scale and testing restricted quantum kernels designed to avoid exponential concentration, including noise effects.
result: Even at small scale, overfitting can collapse GPR performance, and because the quantum fidelity kernel is smooth, regularization must be delicately balanced between expressivity and overfitting; some noise types can even be beneficial.
conclusion: Quantum kernels for GPR require careful regularization, and the qualitative findings transfer to practical restricted kernels and near-term noisy devices.

title: Momentum-resolved Quantum Noise Spectroscopy Using Ensembles Of Diamond Quantum Sensors
authors: Zeeshawn Kazi, Kai-Hung Cheng, Jared Rovny, Nathalie P. de Leon
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09571v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatiotemporal fluctuations across multiple scales govern and characterize the emergent properties, phase boundaries, and low-energy excitations of strongly correlated matter. However, capturing these dynamics has remained a major experimental challenge, as conventional probes typically offer either high spatial or temporal resolution, but not both simultaneously. Here, we leverage high-fidelity wide-field imaging of dense diamond nitrogen vacancy center ensembles to measure the momentum and frequency power spectral density of magnetic fluctuations. To access spatial wavevectors below the diffraction limit, we tune the sensing volume continuously through optical depletion. This approach enables study of equilibrium and driven fluctuations across three orders of magnitude in spatial scale and tunable frequency bands, providing a direct means to map low-energy, long-wavelength fluctuations in correlated systems.
tldr: Dense diamond NV center ensembles enable momentum-resolved quantum noise spectroscopy of magnetic fluctuations by tuning the sensing volume via optical depletion.
motivation: Spatiotemporal fluctuations in correlated matter require simultaneous high spatial and temporal resolution, which conventional probes cannot easily provide.
method: The authors use wide-field imaging of NV center ensembles and continuously tune the sensing volume through optical depletion to access sub-diffraction spatial wavevectors and measure momentum- and frequency-resolved power spectral densities.
result: The approach captures equilibrium and driven magnetic fluctuations across three orders of magnitude in spatial scale and tunable frequency bands.
conclusion: This provides a direct means to map low-energy, long-wavelength fluctuations in correlated systems, but it remains primarily a quantum sensing/metrology application rather than a contribution to qubit hardware or transduction.

title: ECDSA.Fail: Open Autoresearch For Optimizing Elliptic-Curve Point Addition In Shor's Algorithm
authors: Jieyi Long, Theodore Pender, Zhao Huang, Manuel B. Santos, Samrendra Kumar Singh, Bartosz Naskr\k{e}cki, Bit Wonka, Joe Doyle, Pierre-Luc Dallaire-Demers, Francesco Giannicola, Ruben M. L. Paschoarelli, Oli Freuler, Jackie Chia-Hsun Lee, Vasily Gnuchev, Gopi Kannappan, John Boyer, Xavier Butler, Akash Balasubramani, Jordan Newman, Bereket Dereje, Alexander Hertlein, Robert Kodra, Lucas Levy, Shaan Patel, JT Rose, Matt Zweil, Okechukwu Wisdom, Tarek El-Eter, Edison Lee, Michael Dong, Alan Li, Anto Joseph, Gajesh Naik, Gautham Anant, Soubhik Deb, Justin Drake
abstract: ArXiv:2609.09582v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose Open Autoresearch, a paradigm in which humans and AI agents publish evaluator-verified improvements to a public leaderboard. We instantiate it in ECDSA.Fail, optimizing reversible secp256k1 point-addition circuits, a bottleneck in Shor's algorithm for elliptic-curve cryptography. The benchmark minimizes the spacetime-inspired score [MATH], where [MATH] is peak logical qubit width and [MATH] is average executed Toffoli count. Participants reduced [MATH] by 86.1%. At the data cutoff (26 July 2026), the best-scoring circuit uses 1,151 qubits and 1,299,453 average executed Toffoli gates, giving [MATH] billion. This is more than 50% below Google's published point-addition score thresholds (arXiv:2603.28846), under different accounting conventions. Because the benchmark supplies one addend classically, we construct a coherent windowed-addition-compatible variant implementing the single-call interface required by windowed Shor. It uses 1,162 qubits and 1,684,161 average executed Toffoli gates. On 100,000 random inputs, its empirical success probability is [MATH], giving [MATH] billion under an independently rerunnable per-call sensitivity model, not a full-Shor success estimate. Its qubit and Toffoli counts lie below Google's published thresholds and Schrottenloher's reported operating points (arXiv:2606.02235), although differing interfaces, accounting conventions, and validation scope preclude formal dominance. After the cutoff, the score was further reduced to 1.259 billion, while a separate low-width circuit reached 813 qubits. The public record shows AI agents complementing human judgment, providing evidence for open autoresearch on efficiently evaluable, machine-checkable objectives.
tldr: This paper introduces an open autoresearch benchmark and optimized reversible circuits for secp256k1 elliptic-curve point addition within Shor's algorithm, reducing qubit and Toffoli counts.
motivation: Breaking ECDSA with Shor's algorithm requires efficient quantum circuits for elliptic-curve point addition, making resource estimation a key bottleneck.
method: A public leaderboard task is used where humans and AI agents submit evaluator-verified circuit improvements that minimize a spacetime score based on peak logical qubit width and average executed Toffoli gates; a windowed-addition-compatible variant is also constructed.
